media:group.media:title: IPL mai Child Labour? | #LLAShorts 1535
media:group.media:description:
Some FIRs are filed for justice. Some are filed just for attention.
A recent debate started after questions were raised about whether a 15 year old cricketer like Vaibhav Suryavanshi should even be playing professional cricket under Indian labour laws. The argument was that minors are meant to study, not participate in commercial sports leagues.
But the legal reality is more nuanced than viral statements make it sound. India’s labour laws do restrict hazardous child labour, but they also allow minors to work in specific fields under regulated conditions. Sports, entertainment and creative professions often operate through guardians and supervised contracts because contracts signed directly with minors are generally not enforceable under Indian contract law.
The bigger irony is that authorities already struggle to address serious labour violations happening across the country every day. So the chances of enforcement agencies suddenly prioritising a teenage cricketer earning through a professional sports system are realistically quite low.
Some issues deserve outrage. Some deserve legal action. And some simply become social media noise because they are attached to a famous name.
The internet reacts very selectively. Real problems are ignored quietly, while symbolic controversies become national debates overnight.
What do you think about this entire issue? Drop your opinion in the comments and share this with someone following the debate closely. Stay Jagruk.

media:group.media:title: Name Change ka PLAN FAIL! | #LLAShorts 1533
media:group.media:description:
Fix bullying… but ended up getting trolled instead.
A campaign was introduced in Rajasthan aiming to reduce bullying among school children by encouraging more meaningful names. The idea was simple: if a child’s name could become a reason for teasing, schools could work with parents to change it to something more respectful and positive.
On paper, it sounded thoughtful. Prevent embarrassment early, avoid confidence issues later. A reference list of thousands of “better” names was even shared to guide the process.
But things didn’t go as planned.
Some of the suggested names in that list raised eyebrows instantly. Instead of solving the problem, it created a new one. Social media picked it up, criticism started pouring in, and the entire campaign faced heavy backlash.
Eventually, the initiative had to be rolled back. The intent may have been right, but execution matters just as much. Not every problem has a simple fix, and definitely not one that can be solved by a list.
What’s your take on this idea? Smart move or overreach? Drop your thoughts in the comments and share this with someone who has an interesting nickname story. Stay Jagruk.

media:group.media:title: Famous at What Cost? | #LLAShorts 1528
media:group.media:description:
Bet you didn’t know about this .
What feels like everyday language is often just clever branding that became too popular. Words like bandage, xerox, fevicol or even geyser are not actually the real names of the products. They started as brand names, but over time people began using them for the entire category.
This is where things get interesting. When a brand becomes so famous that it replaces the actual product name in daily use, it enters a zone called “generic trademark”. At that point, the brand risks losing its exclusive identity because people no longer see it as a brand, they see it as the product itself.
It has already happened globally with names like aspirin and escalator. Once protected trademarks, now common terms anyone can use. And if the same pattern continues, even popular names we use in India today could face a similar situation in the future.
So next time you casually say a brand name, there is a good chance you are not naming the product correctly.
Let’s make this interesting Drop the real product names for the items you see in the video in the comments
Share this with someone who still says xerox instead of photocopy, and follow for more such insights. Stay Jagruk.

entry.title: Ab Foreign Trip pe bhi Tax? | #LLAShorts 1526

media:group.media:title: Ab Foreign Trip pe bhi Tax? | #LLAShorts 1526
media:group.media:description:
Travel abroad… but only after paperwork?
A new rule under the Income Tax Act 2025 brings an extra layer before international travel for a specific set of people. Anyone without a PAN, those not required to have one, or individuals whose income isn’t even taxable may need to submit a Form 157 before leaving the country.
On paper, it sounds like a simple compliance step. In reality, it’s not just a quick online form. It involves physically filling it, visiting the jurisdictional officer, and getting it submitted every single time someone plans to travel abroad. And this doesn’t just stop at one person. In many households, even if one member is a taxpayer, others like spouse, parents, or children may still fall under this requirement.
The intention may be to track financial activity, but the process raises practical concerns. Repeating the same offline procedure for every trip can become a hassle, especially when travel plans are time-sensitive.
Miss it, and there could be consequences ranging from inconvenience at the airport to further notices later.
This is where policy meets real-life execution, and that gap is what people are questioning.
What’s your take on this rule? Necessary control or unnecessary friction? Share your thoughts in the comments and pass this on to someone who travels abroad frequently. Stay Jagruk.
